title: Health and enough
hook: health is the greatest gift, contentment the greatest wealth (Dhammapada 204)
tomorrow: why would a poem compare a good life to a tree?

segments.voice: Yesterday, three lines of teaching: avoid, do, purify, easy to know and hard to do. Today, the last of these Dhammapada verses, and an argument.

One side of the feed says hustle, the other says slow down, and both are selling something. Is wanting more a problem, or the point? The Dhammapada's verse two hundred and four, in Max Müller's translation: "Health is the greatest of gifts, contentedness the best riches." Sounds settled. But inside the Buddhist tradition, enough has two sides, and the story behind this verse starts at a royal dinner table.
screen: `HUSTLE, OR SLOW DOWN?` → `HEALTH, THE GREATEST GIFT.` → `ENOUGH HAS TWO SIDES.`

segments.voice: In the Samyutta Nikaya, King Pasenadi of Kosala has a habit: he eats huge meals. One day he comes to the Buddha straight from the table, heavy and huffing. The Buddha offers a short verse: a person who is mindful and knows the measure in eating grows old slowly and keeps their life. The king has his nephew recite it at every meal. Little by little he eats less, grows lighter, and one day, stroking his own limbs, says the Buddha has been kind to him twice over. View one, then: contentment. The Buddha praises a monk who is content with his robe and his bowl, carrying them the way a bird carries only its wings. Its best case: craving never fills, and enough is the only wealth no one can take. Now view two. In another sutta the Buddha says he learned two things on his way to awakening: not to rest content with the good qualities he had, and not to give up striving. Its best case: contentment can become an excuse, and the path asks you to keep going. Both are the Buddha's own words. Some teachers put them together like this: be content with things, and never content with how far you've grown. Enough bread; not enough kindness. Bread and growth are different hungers, and the tradition keeps both views.
screen: `THE KING WHO ATE TOO MUCH.` · `VIEW ONE: A BIRD WITH ONLY ITS WINGS.` · `VIEW TWO: DON'T REST CONTENT.` · `ENOUGH THINGS; NOT ENOUGH GROWTH.` · then, large: `CONTENTMENT IS WEALTH.`

segments.voice: Rest one hand on your belly and breathe. Notice that each in-breath stops on its own when it's full; you don't have to force more in. Let that be enough, breath after breath. If some part of you is hurting, rest the hand wherever it's comfortable instead.
Health and enough: the Dhammapada's greatest gift and best riches. Content with things, and still growing.
Your line: contentment is wealth, in what you have, not in who you've become. Ten days of verses, and the book closes for now.

howItsDone: Buddhist monks and nuns keep few possessions and eat within set limits, practicing contentment (santutthi); teachers pair it with steady effort (viriya) in practice, so that contentment with things never becomes contentment with oneself.

fork.setup: you lean toward view one: contentment is wealth. now state view two, 'don't rest content', at its strongest.
options: contentment can turn into an excuse; the path asks you to keep striving.

fork.reveal: view two's best case is the Buddha's own: he didn't rest content with his good qualities, and he didn't give up striving. both views are his.

what it means: content with things, which is real wealth, and never content with how far you've grown.
what a scholar hears: Dhammapada 204's story of King Pasenadi, the monk content as a bird with its wings, and the Buddha's 'discontent with skillful qualities'.
guess: being satisfied with what you have, as true riches

chat.says: theo took extra shifts again. says 'enough' is for people who quit trying. is he right?
options: Half right. The Buddha said: content with things, never with your growth.
Yes. The Buddha said never be content; always reach for more.
No. Contentment means wanting nothing at all, not even to grow.
chat.meaning: Both views are the Buddha's: be content with robe and bowl, and don't rest content with your good qualities. Things and growth are different hungers.

tie.story: The Buddha praised a monk content as a bird with its wings, and also said he never rested content with his good qualities.
tie.friend: Zoe can tell Theo striving to grow is fine; more shifts for more things is a different hunger.
tie.you: where are you content, and where are you still growing?

Pasenadi.meaning: a king of Kosala and a lay follower of the Buddha

Kosala.meaning: a kingdom of northern India in the Buddha's time

Samyutta Nikaya.meaning: the Connected Discourses, a Pali collection of suttas

awakening.meaning: the Buddha's waking up to the truth, his enlightenment
